summary: A satirical article mocking cybersecurity training for remote employees and its attempts to reduce human error. It pokes fun at dull webinars, predictable simulated phishing, frequent password changes, gamification and advanced security tools. It ends by refusing to offer a neat conclusion, arguing that training rarely makes employees or companies fully safe.
one_line: A satirical take on remote-work cybersecurity training, lampooning webinars, phishing simulations, password rules, gamification and security tools as ineffective against human error.
key_facts: On 15 September 2023, John Smith, IT manager at SecureTech Solutions, launched a new cyber-awareness initiative.
Smith's centerpiece was a 90-minute webinar covering password policies and data encryption tactics, which failed to hold remote employees' attention.
The article jokes that collective gasps at learning the difference between strong and weak passwords sound like muted snoring.
Since 22 October 2023, when Mary Johnson of Acme Corp received her first 'urgent email from the CEO', employees have been forwarding simulated phishing emails to IT.
The article claims simulated phishing tests have become as predictable as a soap opera plot, with staff swapping tales of narrow escapes involving the Prince of Nigeria.
Companies now mandate quarterly password changes for remote employees, which the article says leads to lockouts when people forget whether they used an ampersand or a percent sign.
Gamification of cyber training uses leaderboards, points and badges, but remote workers have no watercoolers to talk about them.
The article jokes that Jane in accounting beat a colleague for the top score by spotting a scam email about free pizza in the break room.
On November 29, 2023, firms introduced advanced cybersecurity tools, which employees are said to bypass inadvertently despite promises of ease of use.
Employees are jokingly described as sobbing over keyboards while trying to remember which of seven security questions they answered incorrectly.
The conclusion section says conclusions are not allowed, since they would falsely suggest employees emerge enlightened, bad actors reform and companies become forever safe from cyber attacks.
